claims.text: Section title and scope: 50 U.S.C. 3348, 'Reports relating to certain special access programs and similar programs'. Codified from Pub. L. 103-160, div. A, title XI, sec. 1152, Nov. 30, 1993, 107 Stat. 1758; formerly classified as a note under 50 U.S.C. 435 before editorial reclassification.

THE COVERAGE HOLE. 3348(g)(2)(B): the term 'covered department or agency' 'does not include-- (i) the Department of Defense (which is required to submit reports on special access programs under section 119 of title 10); (ii) the National Nuclear Security Administration (which is required to submit reports on special access programs under section 2426 of this title); or (iii) an agency in the Intelligence Community (as defined in section 3003(4) of this title).' The government-wide SAP reporting statute therefore reaches none of the three communities where a legacy recovery program would plausibly sit.

3348(e)(1): 'The head of a covered department or agency may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report ... if the head of the department or agency determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis.' (e)(2) requires the withheld information and the waiver justification to be provided 'to the congressional oversight committees' -- with no reduction to chairs and ranking members.

3348(f): 'A special access program may not be initiated by a covered department or agency until-- (1) the congressional oversight committees are notified of the program; and (2) a period of 30 days elapses after such notification is received.'

3348(g)(1) defines 'congressional oversight committees' as congressional leadership and the authorizing and appropriations committees with jurisdiction or shared jurisdiction over the department or agency, plus the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs and the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform (now Oversight and Accountability). This definition was ADDED by Pub. L. 115-390 sec. 103(3) in December 2018; before that the statute said only 'Congress'.

3348(g)(3) still defines 'special access program' by reference to 'Executive Order 12356 (or any successor Executive order)' — an order revoked in 1995 by E.O. 12958 sec. 6.1(d), as the GPO 'References in Text' note states. The operative definition today runs through the successor chain to E.O. 13526.

claims.text: The section heading is 'Reports relating to certain special access programs and similar programs'. The word doing the work is 'certain': DoD, NNSA and the Intelligence Community are routed out of it by subsection (g)(2)(B) to their own regimes, and the DoD regime it routes to, 10 U.S.C. 119, is the one carrying a waiver.

50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(3) defines 'special access program' as 'any program that, under the authority of Executive Order 12356 (or any successor Executive order), is established by the head of a department or agency whom the President has designated in the Federal Register as an original "secret" or "top secret" classification authority that imposes "need-to-know" controls or access controls beyond those controls normally required ... for access to information classified as "confidential", "secret", or "top secret".'

50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(1) defines 'congressional oversight committees' to include 'the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform of the House of Representatives' and the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, as well as congressional leadership and the authorizing and appropriations committees with jurisdiction.

50 U.S.C. 3348(e)(2): where the waiver is exercised, the agency head 'shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, to the congressional oversight committees' - the full committees, not a chair and ranking member.
50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(2)(B) excludes from 'covered department or agency' only the Department of Defense, the National Nuclear Security Administration and agencies in the Intelligence Community.

claims.text: Section 3348 was enacted as Pub. L. 103-160, div. A, title XI, sec. 1152, 30 November 1993, 107 Stat. 1758, and amended by Pub. L. 115-390, sec. 103, 21 December 2018, which substituted 'the congressional oversight committees' for 'Congress' throughout and added the definition of that term.

Any special access program run by DHS, DOE outside NNSA, NASA, Commerce, Justice or any other non-excluded agency is reportable by statute to the House Oversight Committee - which means House Oversight's UAP subpoenas and document demands rest on a statutory entitlement that has not been publicly invoked. Reasoning: 3348(g)(1)(C) names the committee and (g)(2) excludes only three categories of agency.

desc: Section 1152 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1994, Public Law 103-160 of 30 November 1993, now codified at 50 U.S.C. 3348, is the sleeper statute of this whole architecture and it is almost never cited in UAP reporting. It imposes on the head of every 'covered department or agency' the same February 1 annual report, new-program notice, 14-day declassification notice and 30-day report-and-wait that 10 U.S.C. 119 imposes on the Secretary of Defense - and it defines 'covered department or agency' as 'any department or agency of the Federal Government that carries out a special access program', excluding only DoD (covered by 10 U.S.C. 119), the National Nuclear Security Administration (covered by 50 U.S.C. 2426) and 'an agency in the Intelligence Community'. Two provisions make it invaluable. First, it supplies the statutory definition of a special access program: 'any program that, under the authority of Executive Order 12356 (or any successor Executive order), is established by the head of a department or agency whom the President has designated in the Federal Register as an original "secret" or "top secret" classification authority that imposes "need-to-know" controls or access controls beyond those controls normally required ... for access to information classified as "confidential", "secret", or "top secret".' Second, as amended by section 103 of Public Law 115-390 on 21 December 2018, 'congressional oversight committees' means 'congressional leadership and authorizing and appropriations congressional committees with jurisdiction or shared jurisdiction over a department or agency', the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, AND the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform of the House of Representatives. The House Oversight Committee - the committee that has run the public UAP hearings since July 2023 - is a named statutory recipient of special access program reports from every covered agency. And its waiver provision, subsection (e)(2), does not narrow the audience: the waived information still goes 'to the congressional oversight committees', not to a chair and ranking member. The non-defense SAP reporting regime is materially stronger than DoD's.

timeline.label: The government-wide SAP statute and the only statutory definition
timeline.text: Section 1152 of the FY1994 NDAA, Public Law 103-160, imposes the same reporting regime on every federal agency that runs a SAP other than DoD, the nuclear weapons complex and the intelligence community, and supplies the only statutory definition of 'special access program' in the United States Code, now at 50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(3).

timeline.label: House Oversight named a statutory recipient of SAP reports
timeline.text: Section 103 of Public Law 115-390 amends 50 U.S.C. 3348 to substitute 'the congressional oversight committees' for 'Congress' throughout and defines that term to include the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform and the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
